title: About the End of the World: Crises of Cosmopolitanism in Contemporary Culture and Theory
subject: SPANSH
description: Cosmopolitanism and globalization, two master-concepts that were extremely useful to understand subjective universalistic desires and material processes of global dislocation, disjuncture and displacement (as well as fantasies of totality, transparent communication and interrelations, and fictions of totality) can no longer account for our present cultural-political situation; they are not useful to interrogate the global displacements and traumatic losses constitutive of the overwhelming…
fullDescription: Cosmopolitanism and globalization, two master-concepts that were extremely useful to understand subjective universalistic desires and material processes of global dislocation, disjuncture and displacement (as well as fantasies of totality, transparent communication and interrelations, and fictions of totality) can no longer account for our present cultural-political situation; they are not useful to interrogate the global displacements and traumatic losses constitutive of the overwhelming experience, over the last few years, that we are living through the end of the world. The idea of end of the world does not refer only to the sense of overwhelming political futility that dominates the artistic and intellectual spheres today, but also to the collapse of the world understood as the modern/modernist symbolic structure that supported humanist discourses of universal emancipation through global connections, translations, interactions, displacements and exchanges; the world as the symbolic realm where demands of justice, emancipation and universal inclusion were meant to be actualized. Today, the displacement of more than 67 millions refugees, migrants and forcibly displaced persons as a result of environmental catastrophes, economic hardships, and small and large scale perpetual wars and terror in Latin America, Africa, the Middle East and Europe; the theatrical demolition of liberal democratic governmentality in Trump's America and across the Western hemisphere; the crisis or death of Europe as a project of political and cultural reorientation of the American global hegemony; the painful intensification of the military, economic and symbolic violence the Israeli state exerts over Palestinian people; and the radicalization of financial capital’s global sovereignty since the “recovery” from the 2008 crisis and the subsequent concentration of wealth and global socio-economic inequality―all these point to the radical dislocation of the structure we used to call "world". But this course is not about the very real historical suffering and losses of those whose bodies are wounded by the end of the world; it is rather about the trace of those experience that we call art and literature; about some of the idiosyncratic ways in which those of us who care about art and literature attend to these forms as symbolic sites in order to try and fail to understand the end of the world; about our reaction to an experience of the end of the world that is and is not our end of the world; and about what we (we professors, students, intellectuals, writers, artists) can and can no longer do about the end of the world through art as mediation. In order to work through these notions we read texts by Roberto Bolaño, Imannuel Kant, Yuri Herrera, Hannah Arendt, Homi Bhabha, Jason de León, Maurice Blanchot, Jesús Carrasco, Giorgi Agamben, Georges Didi-Huberman, Samantha Schweblin, Svetlana Boym, Cuathémoc Medina, Raqs Media Collective, Enzo Traverso, Sigmund Freud, Hernán Díaz, Julia Kristeva, Verónica Gerber Bicecci, Olga Tokarczuk, Bonnie Honig, César Aira, Walter Benjamin, Lina Meruane, Mike Wilson, Dipesh Chakrabarty, Bettina Keizman, Ursula K. Heise, Bruno Latour, Irmgard Emmelheinz; we think with the visual work of Bouchra Khalili, Francis Alÿs, Daniel Richter, Leila Alaoui and Daniel Castro García; and we analyze films by Alejandro Brugués (Juan de los Muertos), Jia Zhangke (The World), Lars von Trier (Melancholia), Alfonso Cuarón (Children of Men), and the Brazilian Netflix series "3%".

title: Introduction to Latin American Studies: Aesthetics, Politics, and Anxieties

In the recent history of Latin America, there are multiple instances where aesthetics and politics have intertwined in…
fullDescription: The photographic installations of the Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo, the debates sparked by the farcical intervention in images of national heroes like Emiliano Zapata, or even the hyper-aestheticization of narco culture on social media, in films, and series, all serve as evidence that the politics of a region cannot be understood without its art, literature, and culture. In the recent history of Latin America, there are multiple instances where aesthetics and politics have intertwined in order to create and find new meanings for the issues plaguing the region. If a citizen participates in both the action of being governed and the action of governing, there is no doubt that aesthetics, understood as the formal exploration of the distribution of the sensible, as Rancière would say, is a productive space for analysis to understand Latin American intellectual and political traditions. In this course, we will panoramically explore the relationship between aesthetics and politics throughout the 19th, 20th, and 21st centuries in Latin America. By studying cinema, literature, art, music, and more, the objective is to offer students an approach to how art and culture bear witness, often in a more visceral and affective way than is possible from a purely historiographical or sociological approach, to what politics cannot resolve. We will analyze and discuss Latin American productions based on key aesthetic concepts (manifesto, declamation, performance, documentary, etc.), in order to trace and outline the anxieties plaguing both art and contemporary Latin American criticism.

fullDescription: This course introduces statistical inference and computing through applications in public health, medicine, and the life sciences. Topics include data visualization, data wrangling, principles of data collection, probability, estimation, hypothesis testing, and regression modeling. Students will develop both technical skills and statistical literacy, with a strong awareness of the ethical issues that arise when collecting, analyzing, and communicating data. The course prepares students to be responsible statistical practitioners, equipped to learn and apply field-specific methods while critically evaluating how analyses are conducted and how results are communicated. Active learning is central to the course: students prepare through videos and pre-class assignments, then engage in collaborative problem-solving during class meetings. Students will learn a reproducible workflow for analyzing data with the statistical language R. No prior statistics or programming experience is required.

fullDescription: A second course in Statistics -- analyzing sports data using data science tools. Commonly used measures and practices will be introduced to illustrate modern sports analytic thinking. The course will cover visualizing, analyzing, and modeling data from team and individual sports and other competitive games. Communicating these results to less technical audiences will be a focus. Modules will include methods for player, team, and coach evaluation; game planning; and decision making. The course assumes prior statistical and computing knowledge at the Stat 100/102/104 level including the use of R. No prior knowledge of sports analytics is necessary, but students should have, or be interested in obtaining, a basic understanding of the rules and terminology used in major team and individual sports.

This class will include 4 modules. The first module introduces the nuanced world of causal inference along with a…
fullDescription: Causal inference concerns the very difficult, challenging problem of addressing questions such as, "Would vaccinating children 16 and younger against COVID 19 lead to fewer deaths among public school teachers?" and "Would providing Harvard students access to a mobile health application designed to help them manage school stress, lead to improved school performance?" This class will include 4 modules. The first module introduces the nuanced world of causal inference along with a fundamental tool: the language of potential outcomes. The second module covers randomized experiments and how data from randomized experiments can be used to make causal statements. The third module introduces the rather tricky problem of using observational (non-randomized) data to attempt to make causal statements. The final module introduces a new and challenging area in which the goal is to make causal inference about the effect of sequences of treatments.

fullDescription: This graduate course will focus on reinforcement learning algorithms and sequential decision making methods with special attention to how these methods can be used in mobile health. Reinforcement learning is the area of machine learning which is concerned with sequential decision making. We will focus on the areas of sequential decision making that concern both how to select optimal actions as well as how to evaluate the impact of these actions. The choice of action is operationalized via a policy. A policy is a (stochastic) deterministic mapping from the available data at each time t into (a probability space over) the set of actions. We will consider both off-line and on-line methods for learning good policies. Mobile health is an area that lies within multiple scientific disciplines including: statistical science, computer science, behavioral science and cognitive neuroscience. This makes for very exciting interdisciplinary science! Smartphones and wearable devices have remarkable sensing capabilities allowing us to understand the context in which a person is at a given moment. These devices also have the ability to deliver treatment actions tailored to the specific needs of users in a given location at a given time. Figuring out when and in which context, which treatment actions to deliver can assist people in achieving their longer term health goals. In multiple classes we will brainstorm about how the methods we discussed during that class might be useful in mobile health. This course will cover the following topics: Markov Decision Processes, on-policy and off-policy RL, least squares methods in RL and Bayesian RL, namely posterior sampling. Most of the course will focus on Bayesian RL via posterior sampling. This is particularly useful in mobile health as posterior sampling facilitates off-policy and continual learning. Also the Bayesian paradigm facilitates use of prior data in initializing an RL algorithm. Other topics from statistics, machine learning and RL that I think are interesting (you could consider in your class project) include: 1) transfer learning (using data on other similar users to enable faster learning); 2) RL for steering LLM behavior; 3) interpretability of policies (enabling communication with behavioral scientists by making connections to behavioral theories); 4) methods for warm-starting RL algorithms, 5) hierarchical RL, 6) experience replay and 7) multi-task learning.

fullDescription: Course Description: Deep statistics refers to statistical endeavors that go deeper than developing methods and applying them to solve problems in data science. It explores and develops statistical theory and insights to contribute to the building of foundations for data science. The course provides a deep dive into statistical foundations and insights for multi-source, multi-phase, and multi-resolution learning, interwoven with case studies on using AI and Earth Observations (EO) for sustainable developments (e.g., global poverty). Foundational issues are framed as inevitable trade-offs for data science: between data quality and quantity, between statistical and computational efficiencies, and between robustness and relevance of learning methods and findings. Practical questions examined include handling messy and private data, drawing causal conclusions from AI-EO data, and translating scientific insights into policies.

fullDescription: This is an acting class designed both for students who have had no previous acting, performance, or any arts class experience, as well as for students who have had a fair amount of acting experience. The focus is on monologue and scene work using classical texts and contemporary texts from theater, television and film. Core components of the course include the idea of navigating a situation as you actually would in real life, how to read a monologue or scene to figure out what your character might want from a situation, “action-based acting” (how a person might go about getting what they want from the other person), how to find a personal connection to a character, and how to choose material that best suits the individual actor for scene work and auditions. It is important to note that while the class will focus on tangible and concrete acting techniques and is intentionally designed to be un-intimidating, it does require a great deal of outside work. Students should expect to spend 4-6 hours per week outside of class, including memorization and rehearsal time for scenes and monologues.

fullDescription: For students interested in working in theater, film, and television, this course applies advanced voice and speech skills to plays and other text written in heightened language. Building on foundational skills of breath release, resonance, and articulation, this class will integrate these skills with text and character analysis, culminating in several performances throughout the semester. We will investigate poetry, monologues and scenes by Sophocles, Langston Hughes, Kate Hamill, George Bernard Shaw, August Wilson, Caryl Churchill, and William Shakespeare, among others. In parallel with the exploration of voice and language, we will examine different mediums in which actors might perform these texts, in outdoor performance venues, proscenium theaters, and in small spaces in front of cameras. We will experiment with the changing demands on our voices in these changing relationships with space and audience. Students will gain confidence in performance and greater skill in using their voices to bring language alive.

fullDescription: This course is a continuation of "Physical Approaches to Acting and Storytelling." Focus will continue to be on principles and practices of performative movement as it expands to include a compact survey of the global ritual underpinnings of movement performance (from the paleolithic era to present). Basic techniques will be introduced from selected performance traditions from Sanskrit, Kabuki, Kathakali theater traditions to Butoh dance, Grotowski's movement lab, Scott Graham’s “Frantic Method” and Joshua Fried's headphone work. We will discuss how material may be generated through these performance methods (and will engage parallel discussion about the ethics of using quoted movement from cultural ritual and performance traditions). We will both investigate and physicalize the practices and methods of devised theater from the early 20th century to present (with a particular focus on the Dada and Futurist movements of 1910’s-20’s, as well as on the methods of Bertolt Brecht). Short Futurist and Dadaist scripts will be analyzed and performed as spoken text becomes more prevalent in composing classwork. Students will write a short paper on three generative techniques covered in class and will research--or create--a fourth generative technique (from any art form) and present/discuss briefly in class (and possibly physicalize, depending on the nature of the technique). Utilizing deeper levels of Viewpoints work, Richard Maxwell and BMG's 6-Archeypte Wheel, the Frantic Method and contact improvisation we'll explore more complex qualities of character, identity, archetype, mannerism, linguistic disfluencies (verbal and non-verbal) and psychological subtext. We will shortly immerse in the world of comedy improv w/ a series of games and exercises designed to deepen intuitive 'play' impulses, deepen ensemble cohesiveness and provide more methods for material generation. We will also briefly explore Rasa Boxes as an improvisational tool. Daily class time will often involve some sort of performance or improvisation by individuals or assigned small groups, culminating in final performance projects at the end of the semester. Along the way, we will continue practice of simple yoga flow sequences, Taoist tai chi and other body practices geared toward conditioning/lengthening/ strengthening the physical instrument. The class will be both rigorously physical and dialogic...and often fun!

fullDescription: Directing Lab: Directing is painting with bodies in space. It requires compositional, emotional, literary and dramaturgical consideration. This practical, foundational directing course invites students to discover a distinctive artistic voice and perspective. We will explore directing as a practice of curiosity, collaboration and discovery. Each week, students will read a play, choose a scene to direct, cast their fellow classmates and rehearse the scene independently to present the following week. The course is oriented around performance that holds all its elements in equal value: when text, performance, movement, space, and design are interconnected elements of a unified artistic vision. "Artistic Literacy," a shared vocabulary of major artists and their works, will provide a bedrock for our conversations. Careful reading of dramatic texts by writers such as Maria Irene Fornés, Tennessee Williams, and Caryl Churchill will inspire a deeper understanding of how form shapes meaning and where dramatic tension resides.

fullDescription: Contemporary puppet theater approaches design and devising from a holistic perspective. All objects onstage contribute to a total performing world. Characters, scenery, and even the stage itself may all be manipulated by hand to become animate, performing beings. Through the lens of puppetry, students are invited to consider how all theater might use visual design elements as active storytellers. Students are guided through the creation and performance of two puppet shows, each in a different style. The first project examines the possibilities of toy theater. Originally a nineteenth century European tradition, it includes a focus on the design of the theater itself (in miniature), and historically, all scenery and characters are flat. In contemporary toy theater, size and dimensionality vary, but a focus on performing scenery and stage effects is retained. The second project explores shadow puppetry. With ancient Asian roots, shadow puppetry exists across the world today in a multitude of forms. This class utilizes a combination of overhead projectors, handheld light sources, paper cut outs, printed images, live drawing, and varied projection surfaces. Projects are informed by examples of contemporary puppet theater as well as theories of art and visual perception, theater scenography, cinema and comics. Classes are divided into varied length segments of discussion, puppet theater construction, play and performing. The class explores devising theater with music, text, or image as core inspiration and alternative models of story structure. Projects investigate different modes of collaboration and varied approaches to the performing puppeteer. Homework includes simple puppet construction, devising and rehearsing original performances, as well as short readings and viewings to complement the practical creation. Grades are assessed by students’ investment in their own artistic and technical growth, attempts to integrate concepts and techniques explored in class into puppet shows, approach towards supportive collaboration inside and outside the classroom, focus, and willingness to try new things and take artistic risks. After completing this course students will have gained valuable skills for devising theater and performance without a script both solo and in a group, incorporating the storytelling capacity of inanimate objects and scenery, utilizing the metaphors inherent to the actor-puppeteer character, and generating strong visual imagery that truly performs onstage.

fullDescription: The goal of this course is to use AI agents in a theatrical context. Its core assumption, which we will test throughout the semester, is that creating an AI agent is like creating a dramatic character: both are artificial entities with which audiences interact. We’ll first explore this similarity historically and conceptually, through acting theories, movement systems, and dramatic texts from the first machine age, a period in the early 20th century when theater sought to catch up with the Industrial Revolution. In the second part of the semester, we’ll use this theoretical armature to tackle AI. We’ll explore how to create custom chatbots and agents (no coding experience required) and experiment with how to deploy them in a theatrical context. This second part is practice-based and experimental (no theatrical experience required). The goal is not to create a polished theatrical piece, but to gain experience with AI tools and explore how to use them (and how not to use them) in a theatrical context. Materials include Léger, Chaplin, Bergson, Meyerhold, Taylor, Treadwell, Stanislavski, Shaw, Ovid and others.

fullDescription: Students will gain facility with reading, speaking, performing, and directing Shakespeare through a simple task: attempting to stage the first act of Shakespeare's Hamlet. Hamlet comes with a lot of baggage. First performed in 1601, the subject of infinite interpretation and adaptation, it sits squarely at the center of Anglophone culture, considered the greatest English play by the English language's greatest playwright. But underneath all that baggage there's a script, a script that assumes certain things about human nature, power, grief, and the public. How do we discover those assumptions? How do we communicate them to an audience? How can a 500-year-old play, written in arcane English, become an experience as compelling as sports, the movies, or a video game? We'll attempt to answer these questions using just the text, our bodies, our voices, and the minimal resources of the theater. This workshop course is open to all students. No previous experience with literary studies, performing, or directing is required. The workshop culminates in an invited performance, after which Shakespeare, Hamlet, and Renaissance drama generally will hopefully feel more approachable both to you and our audience.

fullDescription: Today, Boston and Cambridge are pulsing with dance: from drag shows at Jacques Cabaret to ballets at Citizens Opera House to salsa, samba, West African, and Bollywood classes at the Dance Complex. This course offers an introduction to researching and analyzing the wide range of dance styles that animate Greater Boston’s cultural life, as well as their histories and influence. How might we tell the story of dance in Boston and Cambridge? How has dance here operated as art and entertainment, a medium of self-expression, and a vehicle for social activism, education, community-building, and cultural preservation? Which organizations have supported and funded dance, and to what end? And how can we document the work and experiences of Boston-area dancers, choreographers, and teachers for future posterity? This is a seminar-style, discussion-based course. We will analyze a range of primary sources (dance films, interviews with artists, memoirs, and more) and read essays by cultural historians and theorists to contextualize our observations and arguments. We will also meet with local artists and arts administrators and venture outside the classroom – discovering dance in Harvard’s archives and museums, visiting historic studios and theaters, and watching live performances. No prior experience with dance is necessary to enroll.

fullDescription: This hands-on course serves as a foundation in the art and craft of creative lighting design. Students will explore the medium of light itself and its possibilities in storytelling and world-creation. Introductory exercises in perception and psychology will lead to intensive experimentation with various sources of light to create 2D images or 3D environments. Composition, form, color, time and movement will be explored, as well as the basics of lighting technology. Lighting Design has numerous applications and dimensions, and developing a degree of mastery with light as a medium is useful across many fields. While theatrical lighting equipment will be used in the course, and there will be some discussion of lighting design for performance, our focus will not be exclusively centered around design for the stage.

fullDescription: With the U.S. launch of MTV on August 1, 1981, the media landscape for popular music production and consumption changed irrevocably. With an increased emphasis on visual aesthetics and novel modes of storytelling, the creative expectations of artists and audiences changed in response to new technologies. In this course, we will trace the history of the music video (which began long before the 80s) to understand the evolution of the commercial music industry from early animation and music television through the advent of YouTube and social media. Students will develop an analytical toolbox for interpreting music videos with attention to their visual, sound, and cultural context. The course will cover artists from Madonna and Michael Jackson to Lady Gaga and Kanye West, and media platforms such as MTV, VH1, MySpace, and TikTok. Students will present their own analyses in class, and the semester will culminate in a final project that either presents more in depth analysis or involves the production of their own music videos.

fullDescription: TDM Production Studios consist of a 4-credit course that meets weekly led by TDM Faculty and a full production process led by a professional Director or Choreographer which culminates in the public performance of an original work. TDM’s Spring Theater Production Studio for 2027 will be taught (class) and directed (production) by TDM Artistic Producer, faculty member, and theater maker James Stanley . Stanley makes work in the space of theater, spectacle, clown and experimental comedy. The play we will be working on is TRAGEDY: a tragedy by Will Eno – A satire on the relentlessness of the 24/7 news cycle, this piece from 2000 plays out as a live news broadcast covering the quickly evolving tragedy that no one saw coming: Night is falling! Everyone is disappearing! Will the sun ever rise again? We just… don’t… know! How will our correspondents in the studio, in the field, at home, and at the capital guide us through? Even as they contend with their own dark night of the soul… This production allows us to play with and think about media, putting the M in TDM! If you are interested in exploring the world of theater, spectacle and comedic performance, this may be the TDM Production Studio for you. All levels of experience welcome! This is a play for 5-6 actors. We are also looking for students interested in dramaturgy and assistant directing, though students in these roles may also be asked to perform in small non-speaking roles as part of the newsroom mise en scene. Parts will be cast and roles will be determined from those enrolled in the course. [ALSO NOTE: The balance of characters in this play tends toward the “male.” But that means nothing in the world of the clown, where it’s all drag! In other words, we’ll be making some fun choices. So think broadly about how you might see yourself in this play!]

fullDescription: This course will introduce students to the fundamental issues in and methods of theatre and dance studies. We will engage a number of plays, essays, videos, and live performances to explore the potential of expressive forms, and ask, what can be experienced and known through performance and performing? In doing so, we will address key questions: What constitutes a theatrical event? What are its component parts? What is the relationship between written dramas, scripts, scores, and embodied performance on the stage and in everyday life? What responsibilities do the actors, dancers, directors, choreographers, designers and other members of the production team have to previous incarnation or to an author’s expressed intentions? How does the spectator co-create the meaning of a given production? How does one situate performance historically and from a theoretical perspective? And how can performance become a critical tool to engage cultural, political, and philosophical issues? You will be encouraged to develop your ability to think about performance from many different perspectives and to defend your individual ideas with strong critical skills. Additionally, throughout the course of the semester we will define and demystify the complex terms that operate within this field. This course aims to give students a solid foundation to see, experience and think as performers, as artists, and as scholars of expressive behavior.

fullDescription: How does performance shape gender—especially as it intersects with race and sexuality? And how can gendered performances change the world, creating a new future? “Gender and Performance” engages different—and often conflicting—perspectives to answer these questions. In the first half of the course, we encounter concepts and theoretical tools that enable us to look anew at familiar performances (including those in media, sports, religious and secular rituals, theatre, activism, and our everyday self-presentation). In the second half, we examine activist performances from across a political spectrum. We ask, what forms of performance-based activism are effective, and why?

fullDescription: From matriarchs to monarchs, spiritual mediums to anti-colonial activists, African women have always been central figures in the histories of their societies. In this course we will explore the idea of womanhood across various African communities and think through the ways that the category “woman” changes overtime and functions differently in relation to other social categories like class, age, and religion. Using these key concepts, we will also examine the ways African women participated in, responded to, and contested major historical processes such as slavery, colonialism, and decolonization.

fullDescription: Men to Boys surveys changing images of masculinity in Hollywood films from 1950 to the present. We use the films themselves to chart the enormous changes in how post-World War II culture conceptualized “manhood” and “masculinity.” For instance, the later 1940s and 1950s introduced a softer, wounded American man in films such as The Men and Fear Strikes Out. These changed in the 1960s with the introduction of a “hip,” rebellious male image in popular counterculture films such as Easy Rider and The Graduate. The 1970s saw the rise of the new African American male in Shaft – and a rise in independent African American filmmaking – as well as the emergence of the angry, violent white male protagonist in Taxi Driver. The late 1970s and early 1980s saw this image morph into the conflicted, often working class, white man in Coming Home and Raging Bull, only to splinter into the violent action hero of Die Hard and the vulnerable sexy teenager of Risky Business. By the 1990s, the “Shaft" character had transformed into the more complicated, and human, African American characters in the films of Spike Lee, such as Jungle Fever, and other emerging African American directors. By the mid-1990s, white masculinity was re-defined as juvenile and self-centered by teen-sex comedies such as American Pie. This led directly to the wildly popular comedies celebrating male immaturity of Judd Apatow featuring actors such as Seth Rogin and Jonah Hill. Recently new images of men – morally conflicted heroes saving children, shady lawyers exposing government corruption, comic book super-heroes that have human flaws have emerged – all breaking from and drawing upon former film incarnations of masculinity. The course proceeds chronologically through the films, which we will analyze in the economic, political, sociological, and psychological context in which they were created, and to which they were responding. This will include major historical events such as World War II, the Black Power Movement, Second Wave Feminism, the war in Vietnam, the war in Iraq, as well as the rise and fall of the Cold War. We will contextualize films in the emergence of the counterculture, the collapse of the American economy, the gradual de-stabilization of the middle and working class, and the weakening of the government's moral authority. All of which began with the Vietnam war and continued through Watergate and the Bush administration. Readings from feminist film theorists such as E. Ann Kaplan and from sociological and theoretical essays by Stephanie Coontz, Barbara Ehrenreich, Dorothy Dinnerstein, and Juliet B. Schor will also provide essential context and critique.

Have you ever wondered, for example, why computers and phones bearing an Apple logo seem to be “worth” more than other, similar products? Or why we’re willing to pay more for certain commodities – like blue jeans – that bear a recognizable label? What does it mean when sexuality, gender, race, ethnicity, and other…
fullDescription: Our consumer culture bombards us with images, logos, and representations of human difference; and this bombardment can shape and even manufacture consumer desires and attitudes. Have you ever wondered, for example, why computers and phones bearing an Apple logo seem to be “worth” more than other, similar products? Or why we’re willing to pay more for certain commodities – like blue jeans – that bear a recognizable label? What does it mean when sexuality, gender, race, ethnicity, and other constructs of human identity are used to market certain commodities? As members of a “free market” economy, we often think of ourselves as autonomous agents in a marketplace of endless consumer choices. We might think the consumer choices we make are straightforward reflections of our rational considerations of cost for use value. Yet the billions spent each year on market research reveal that consumers often behave irrationally when faced with a choice of similar products that carry different logos. This course offers conceptual tools and historical context to help us respond in a perceptive and (self) critical manner to effects of the consumer culture(s) we all inhabit. The concept of the “fetish” has a rich past that we will spend time excavating in the interest of grasping its influence as a driver of consumer desire.

fullDescription: Delve into the mystical world of Yiddish folklore and its rich tapestry of supernatural tales. This course explores how Jewish communities have used storytelling to grapple with questions of faith, morality, identity, and the unknown. From the protective yet fearsome golems of medieval lore to the tragic and haunting tales of dybbuks, and the cunning demons that populate folk traditions, students will engage with primary Yiddish texts, translated works, and cinematic adaptations to uncover the cultural and historical contexts of these legends. Through a combination of literary analysis, historical inquiry, and creative interpretation, students will examine the enduring power of these stories in Jewish culture and their influence on broader traditions of magical realism and horror. By the end of the course, participants will have a deeper understanding of how Yiddish supernatural tales reflect communal fears, hopes, and resilience, offering a unique lens into the Jewish imagination and its response to a mysterious and often tumultuous world. No prior knowledge of Yiddish is required; all materials will be provided in translation.

fullDescription: Continuation of Yiddish AA. Introduction to Yiddish language, literature, and culture. In the course of the year, students will acquire a thorough grounding in Yiddish grammar and will develop strong foundational reading, writing, speaking, and comprehension skills.
